[RadPrimer] Biliary tract: gallstones, porcelain gallbladder, gallbladder carcinoma. - [RadPrimer] Hepatic and splenic: calcified hepatic masses, mucinous metastases, splenic/hepatic granulomas, splenic cysts, echinococcal cysts, ischemia/infarct. - [RadPrimer] Pancreatic: chronic pancreatitis and calcified pancreatic masses including solid pseudopapillary neoplasm, mucinous cystic neoplasm, pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor, serous cystadenoma, and pseudocyst. - [RadPrimer] Urinary tract/adrenal: urolithiasis, calyceal diverticulum, calcified renal masses, renal cysts/polycystic kidney disease, renal TB, adrenal parenchymal calcification, calcified adrenal masses, prostatic/vas deferens calcification, bladder calculi, and bladder cancer. - [RadPrimer] Female reproductive organs: calcified uterine leiomyoma, ovarian dermoid/teratoma, ovarian carcinoma. - [RadPrimer] Abdominal wall/soft tissue: injection granulomas, costal cartilage mimic, calcified/ossified scar, calcinosis syndromes. - [RadPrimer] Vascular: arterial calcification/aneurysm, Monckeberg calcification, phleboliths, chronic deep venous thrombosis. - [RadPrimer] Bowel/peritoneum/mesentery: appendicolith, appendiceal mucocele, calcified lymph nodes, sclerosing peritonitis, pseudomyxoma peritonei, lymphangioma, sclerosing mesenteritis. === KEY FACTS === - [Both] Abdominal calcifications visible on radiographs or CT can be grouped by mechanism and morphology rather than by organ alone. - [Both] Metastatic calcification is calcium salt deposition in otherwise normal tissue, classically with hypercalcemia and alkaline pH. - [Both] Dystrophic calcification occurs in damaged tissue after trauma, ischemia, infarction, infection, or tumor. - [Both] Ossification is true bone formation in damaged tissue, such as teratoma or ossified incision scar. - [Both] Concretions form inside vessels or hollow viscera, including gallstones, renal calculi, and phleboliths; they often have a continuous rim or laminated edge. - [Both] Conduit-wall calcification follows tubular structures, producing ringlike or tram-track morphology in arteries, aneurysms, veins, or vas deferens. - [Both] Cystic-wall calcification appears as smooth curvilinear calcification around a fluid-filled mass and is larger than conduit-wall calcification. - [Both] Solid-mass calcification is the most varied category; distribution and matrix help narrow the differential. === ORGAN-BASED CLUES === - [Both] Gallstones vary widely in density. Only a minority are visible on radiographs; calcium bilirubinate stones are more likely to be densely calcified, while cholesterol stones may be isoattenuating to bile. - [Both] Gallstones may be laminated, faceted, or show internal gas. Dropped gallstones after laparoscopic cholecystectomy often settle in dependent recesses such as Morison pouch. - [Both] Porcelain gallbladder is gallbladder wall calcification. The association with gallbladder carcinoma is now considered controversial, and CT is more sensitive than radiography. - [Both] Calcified hepatic masses include hemangioma, adenoma after hemorrhage, fibrolamellar HCC with central scar calcification, conventional HCC, and especially mucinous metastases such as colon cancer. - [Both] Splenic and hepatic granulomas appear as multiple punctate calcifications from healed granulomatous infection, commonly histoplasmosis or TB. - [Both] Acquired splenic cysts are more likely than congenital cysts to show peripheral wall calcification. - [Both] Chronic echinococcal cysts can show extensive whorled or serpiginous internal calcification; STATdx also shows rim calcification with daughter cysts. - [Both] Chronic pancreatitis produces parenchymal and intraductal calcifications, often with pancreatic atrophy and ductal change. - [Both] Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor is the solid pancreatic mass most likely to calcify, usually centrally and coarsely. - [Both] Mucinous cystic neoplasm, solid pseudopapillary neoplasm, serous cystadenoma, and pseudocyst may calcify; MCN often has peripheral curvilinear calcification and serous cystadenoma can calcify in a central scar. - [Both] Renal calculi are opaque on CT except indinavir stones; radiographs miss lucent urate stones and smaller stones. - [Both] Calcified renal masses include RCC, Wilms tumor, and multilocular cystic nephroma; RCC calcification is reported in about 25% of cases. - [Both] Renal cyst calcification is often thin or smooth, but thick, irregular, or nodular calcification raises Bosniak concern. - [Both] Chronic renal TB can cause an atrophic, calcified nonfunctioning kidney, sometimes called putty kidney. - [Both] Adrenal calcification usually reflects old hemorrhage or infection, especially TB or histoplasmosis; adrenal masses such as myelolipoma, adrenocortical carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and adrenal cyst can calcify. - [Both] Vas deferens calcification is paired tubular pelvic conduit calcification, most often in insulin-dependent diabetes or older patients. - [Both] Bladder stones usually reflect urinary stasis or migration from the upper tract; they may be large, laminated, rounded, or spiculated. - [Both] Uterine fibroid calcification may be whorled, flocculent, heterogeneous, or popcorn-like. - [Both] Dermoids often contain tooth or bone calcification in a mural nodule, frequently with fat or a fat-fluid level. - [Both] Epithelial ovarian neoplasms, especially serous malignancies, can calcify and may have calcified peritoneal implants. - [Both] Injection granulomas are typically subcutaneous/buttock calcifications and may mimic intraabdominal calcifications on radiographs. - [Both] Calcinosis syndromes can produce extensive soft-tissue and muscular calcification in connective tissue disease, including scleroderma, CREST, lupus, and dermatomyositis. - [Both] Phleboliths are pelvic venous calcifications, often below the iliac spines and sometimes centrally lucent. - [Both] Chronic deep venous thrombosis can calcify the IVC and iliac veins as linear venous calcification. - [Both] Appendicolith is hardened calcified fecal material and may accompany appendicitis; appendiceal mucocele may show curvilinear wall calcification. - [Both] Sclerosing peritonitis from prior peritoneal dialysis manifests as peritoneal thickening and calcification, sometimes encasing bowel. - [Both] Pseudomyxoma peritonei can have punctate or curvilinear mucinous implant calcifications; lymphangioma can show fine wall or septal calcifications. - [Both] End-stage sclerosing mesenteritis can form a left upper quadrant calcified mesenteric mass with tethered bowel and vessels. === SELECTED PRIMARY IMAGE SET === - RadPrimer image 1: Axial CECT shows calcified gallstones in the gallbladder. sourceSelectionPlan.textBackbone: Use RadPrimer as the canonical hierarchy and article backbone. STATdx article text is largely overlapping and is used mainly to reinforce mechanism categories and broaden image examples.
keepFromRadPrimer: Canonical hierarchy, deck routing, and formal differential diagnosis hierarchy.
Mechanism taxonomy: metastatic, dystrophic, ossification, concretion, conduit-wall, cystic-wall, and solid-mass calcification patterns.
All RadPrimer images as selected primary images because they define the canonical teaching backbone.
keepFromSTATdx: STATdx-only supplemental image examples and modality variants: radiographic gallstones/porcelain gallbladder, hepatic/splenic granulomas, renal/adrenal/TB cases, bladder stone variants, fibroid/dermoid radiographs, vascular examples, appendicoliths, and peritoneal/mesenteric variants.

Source-specific captions that add stronger recognition hooks, such as concretion/surface calcification, eggshell calcification, daughter cysts, jackstone/river stones, putty kidney, Monckeberg arterial calcification, and small-bowel encasement in sclerosing peritonitis.
downweightOrSkip: Do not repeat source-identical article prose twice.
Do not use STATdx breadcrumb/deck path for routing.
Archive only the STATdx renderings that are exact duplicates of selected RadPrimer images by stable source image ID and visual evidence.
sourceSelectionPlan.imageCurationPolicy: Exact duplicates may be archived; near duplicates and conceptual replacements remain selected as recognition reinforcement unless visually identical or unusable.
sourceSelectionPlan.duplicateEvidencePolicy: ExactDuplicate decisions require visual evidence from image_evidence files, same stable source image ID, image hashes, or explicit manual/source confirmation. Caption-only or topic-only similarity must be marked uncertain/nearDuplicate and kept primary.

caseClusterGuardrails.atomicClusterRule: Same-patient, follow-up, adjacent-slice, procedure, comparison-view, and time-lapse clusters should remain together unless the archived member is a visually exact duplicate and the selected retained image preserves the teaching context.
